title: Must a woman cover her head when the adhan is given?
headline: The four schools tie head covering to awrah and prayer, not to hearing the adhan

summary.text: None of the four schools makes covering the head a condition of hearing the adhan, and the recent fatwas are nearly unanimous that a woman at home and uncovered may listen and repeat after the muadhin. What changes the ruling is who is present: if a non-mahram man can see her, covering is required, but that is the rule of awrah, not of the adhan.

paragraphs.text: The verse that governs a woman's covering is in Surat al-Nur, and its command concerns the khimar, the head cover itself, telling the believing women to wrap their headcovers over their chests. The Companions differed over the exception, "except that which necessarily appears thereof": Ibn Abbas is reported to have said it means the face and the hands, and this is the reading al-Mughni cites for Malik and al-Shafi'i. Ibn Mas'ud disagreed with him, and al-Buhuti notes the disagreement when recording the Hanbali school's use of the verse.

Aisha's report shows how the first women understood the command in practice: when the verse was revealed, they took their waist-wrappers, tore them from the edges, and covered their heads with them. Surat al-Ahzab gives the reason for the outer garment, and the tafsir attaches it to her leaving the house, "that is more suitable that they will be known and not be abused". Two further verses are used in this discussion: "Take your adornment at every masjid" is the proof al-Marghinani cites for covering in the prayer, reading "adornment" as what covers the awrah at the time of prayer, and "whoever honors the symbols of Allah, indeed, it is from the piety of hearts" is quoted by those who treat covering at the adhan as an act of reverence rather than an obligation.

The hadith that carries the ruling is tied to prayer, not to the call: "Allah does not accept the prayer of any woman who has reached the age of menstruation unless [she is] veiled," graded Sahih by al-Albani, al-Baqi and Zubair Ali Zai. The general statement that a woman is awrah is graded differently by different scholars, which matters because it is the widest text used in this debate: al-Tirmidhi called it hasan gharib, and Shakir, al-Albani and Bashar Awad call it sahih, while the Darussalam grading marks it da'if. The Permanent Committee issued two answers on it: one listing it as da'if with the Darussalam grading, and another affirming it as authentic and explaining that its meaning is about her going out, "for if she goes out, they will desire her".

The only instruction attached specifically to hearing the call is "When you hear the Adhan, repeat what the Muezzin says," and it is about repeating the words. The practical point is sharpened by a passage in the Shafi'i Mughni al-Muhtaj, which rules that the adhan and iqamah of a person whose awrah is uncovered are still valid, "because the purpose is the announcement and it has been achieved, and the prohibition is for another reason". Covering was never made a condition of the adhan itself.

Ibn Rushd reports agreement that covering the awrah is obligatory in principle, with the disagreement over its extent. In the Hanafi books, Ibn Abidin holds that the obligation of covering is general, in prayer and outside it, even when alone on the sound view, and al-Marghinani cites "no prayer for a menstruating woman except with a khimar"; the body is awrah except face, hands and, on the transmitted view, feet. Hearing a sound is not one of the occasions the chapter lists.

The Maliki al-Dasuqi holds that before a non-mahram Muslim man, all of her is awrah but face and hands; in prayer there is a major and a minor awrah, the head, neck, chest and shin being minor, whose uncovering is disliked and repeated within the time, and before women the boundary is navel to knee. The rule is triggered by a viewer, and the adhan adds none.

Al-Nawawi states for the Shafi'is that "all her body is awrah except the face and the hands"; she must cover the whole head, and even the sliver of face next to it, "because the head is awrah", and there are two awrahs, major before non-mahram men and minor before women. No text in the school ties the head cover to the call, and an adhan given uncovered is valid.

In the Hanbali al-Mughni, all but the face is awrah, with two views on the hands; al-Buhuti records that the face and hands are treated as awrah outside the prayer too, with respect to looking, and in ihram she must cover the whole head, since "covering the head is more emphatic". The obligation is framed by presence and by worship, and the adhan is neither.

IslamQA states that putting on the hijab when hearing the adhan has no basis, and that doing it as a religious practice is an innovated matter, since she may listen and repeat while uncovered. Islamweb says it is not compulsory at home, and in a second answer distinguishes the cases: if she is the one calling the adhan or reciting, covering is liked, but if she is merely hearing, "it is neither compulsory nor likeable".

Shaykh Faraz Rabbani, in the Hanafi tradition, answers that it is "neither obligatory nor specifically recommended," while a voluntary expression of respect for a major symbol of the religion is praiseworthy. Sheikh Abdel Khaliq Hasan Ash-Shareef says it is not necessary and not even recommended, since "the rulings of awrah have no relation to hearing the adhan". Mufti Ebrahim Desai writes that in the absence of a non-mahram it is not compulsory, and that covering at the Quran, adhan or a lesson is desirable as an expression of respect.

The Hanafi-leaning Muftionline answers are not uniform: one says "yes, though the adab is that she should cover her head at all times", and another says women are commanded to cover at all times, especially at the adhan, citing a report that angels do not come near a woman whose hair is uncovered. On the neighbouring question of reciting the Quran uncovered, Dar al-Ifta al-Misriyya held that she may recite "with her head uncovered, without dislike", and Ibn Baz and Ibn Uthaymeen both held that covering is not a condition of recitation when no non-mahram is present.

The Permanent Committee drew the line clearly: it is permissible for her to uncover her head among women, among her mahrams, or alone, and "there is no validity to the statement of one who says it is obligatory for her to cover her head in those situations", while uncovering before non-mahram men is not permitted.

The first apparent clash, over "except that which necessarily appears thereof," is not about the hair at all: whether the exception means the face and hands or something narrower changes the ruling on the face and hands only, and every one of the four schools still treats the hair as awrah in front of a non-mahram man. The second is between "the woman is awrah" and the permitted uncovering in privacy, among women and among mahrams; the scholars read the hadith through its own second clause, "when she goes out," and through the verse's list of those before whom adornment may be shown, so the generality is understood as being about her emergence before men, not about every moment of her day.

The third is between calling the practice an innovation and calling it praiseworthy; the objection falls on the belief that it is religiously required, since no text establishes that, while the praise falls on a free act of reverence for a symbol of the religion under 22:32. That is how a Hanafi answer can say "not obligatory, and not specifically recommended" and still call it good. A woman in her kitchen at Maghrib, hair uncovered, alone or with her husband, owes no covering by every school's own boundary, and the Sunnah is to answer the muadhin's words; if a non-mahram man is in the room or can see her, the ruling changes at once, because the awrah rule is now engaged.
